clinicalPearls: Aspiration of a foreign body is most common in toddlers, who explore with their mouths and have immature airway protective reflexes; food items such as nuts and seeds are frequent culprits.
The classic history is a sudden episode of choking, coughing, or gagging in a previously well young child, often while eating or playing with small objects.
Clinical presentation varies with the site and degree of obstruction; a lodged object may produce unilateral wheeze, reduced air entry, or persistent cough.
A witnessed choking event is a strong clue, but the initial episode can be unwitnessed or followed by a symptom-free interval that leads to delayed diagnosis.
Chest radiographs may be normal because most aspirated objects are radiolucent; indirect signs include localised air trapping or hyperinflation, atelectasis, or a persistent infiltrate.
Rigid bronchoscopy is the definitive procedure for both confirming and removing an airway foreign body.
Complete upper airway obstruction is a life-threatening emergency requiring immediate basic choking manoeuvres appropriate to the child's age.
Delayed or missed diagnosis can lead to recurrent or persistent pneumonia, bronchiectasis, or chronic lung damage, so a high index of suspicion is important.
reference.pathophysiology: When a small object is inhaled it may lodge anywhere from the larynx to the distal bronchi, with the site determining the clinical picture. A large object at the larynx or trachea can cause complete or near-complete obstruction and rapid asphyxia. More commonly the object passes into a bronchus, producing partial obstruction: air may move past on inspiration but be trapped on expiration, causing distal hyperinflation, or the airway may become fully blocked, leading to distal atelectasis. Retained material provokes inflammation and, over time, granulation tissue, mucus retention, and secondary infection, which underlie the chronic complications seen with delayed removal.
additionalDifferentials: Croup or other infectious airway obstruction
additionalInvestigations: Chest radiograph including inspiratory and expiratory (or lateral decubitus) views
Assessment for asymmetric air entry or localised findings on examination
Rigid bronchoscopy for diagnosis and removal
Neck radiographs if a laryngotracheal object is suspected
Further imaging when diagnosis remains uncertain despite strong suspicion
redFlags: Complete airway obstruction with inability to cough, speak, or breathe
Cyanosis or rapidly progressive respiratory distress
Stridor with severe distress suggesting a laryngotracheal foreign body
reference.prognosis: With timely recognition and bronchoscopic removal the outlook is generally excellent, whereas complete obstruction can be rapidly fatal and delayed diagnosis may result in chronic pulmonary complications such as bronchiectasis.
pitfalls: Excluding aspiration because the chest radiograph is normal
Being falsely reassured by a symptom-free interval after the initial choking event
Attributing persistent focal respiratory symptoms to recurrent infection or asthma rather than a retained foreign body
Performing blind finger sweeps or inappropriate manoeuvres that may push an object further
